sec.h: Anaemia of chronic disease (anaemia of inflammation)
b: This occurs with prolonged inflammation, chronic infection, autoimmune disease, some cancers and other chronic illnesses.

qs.q: Which iron study pattern is seen in anaemia of chronic disease?
o: Low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC
High ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC
High ferritin, high serum iron, low TIBC
Low ferritin, high serum iron, high TIBC
qs.e: Inflammation sequesters iron in macrophages (high ferritin as acute phase reactant), reduces serum iron, and decreases TIBC — distinguishing it from iron deficiency.

es.q: Explain the pathophysiology of anaemia of chronic disease.
es.m:
- **Cytokine effect** – IL‑1, TNF‑α and other cytokines alter iron metabolism and erythropoiesis.
- **Reduced erythropoietin production and responsiveness** – cytokines blunt renal EPO synthesis and marrow response.
- **Iron sequestration** – increased ferritin, decreased serum iron, low TIBC, and low transferrin saturation despite adequate stores.
- **Decreased transferrin synthesis** – limits iron transport to the marrow.
- **Resulting reticulocytopenia** – inadequate RBC production leads to mild‑to‑moderate anaemia, often normocytic but can become mildly microcytic.

ai.title: Anaemia of Chronic Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) is a mild‑to‑moderate normocytic, normochromic anaemia caused by impaired iron utilisation and blunted erythropoietin response in the setting of inflammation. It is common in low‑resource settings where infections and chronic inflammatory conditions prevail.

sections.p: ACD is defined by a haemoglobin below the age‑adjusted lower limit, with low serum iron, low transferrin (or low transferrin saturation), normal or increased ferritin, and a normal or low reticulocyte count.
b: Normocytic, normochromic picture on peripheral smear
Ferritin ≥100 µg/L (or normal/high) despite low serum iron
Transferrin saturation <20 % (often low‑normal)
Erythropoietin level inappropriately low for degree of anaemia

t.b: Is there anaemia and what is the red cell morphology? – Confirms normocytic, normochromic pattern typical of ACD.

t.a: Serum iron, total iron‑binding capacity (TIBC) and ferritin
t.b: Is iron sequestration present? – Low serum iron, low TIBC, ferritin ≥100 µg/L supports ACD; if ferritin <30 µg/L think iron deficiency.

t.a: C‑reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate
t.b: Is there active inflammation? – Elevated CRP/ESR strengthens ACD diagnosis.
Is marrow response adequate? – Low/normal retic count indicates impaired erythropoiesis.
Is EPO response blunted? – Inappropriately low EPO for degree of anaemia supports ACD.

sections.p: Severity is staged by haemoglobin concentration, guiding urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.
b: Mild: Hb 10–12 g/dL
Moderate: Hb 8–9.9 g/dL
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL (consider transfusion if symptomatic)

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals the most frequent drivers are chronic infections and inflammatory diseases.
b: Chronic infections: HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, schistosomiasis, chronic hepatitis B
Autoimmune/inflammatory disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis
Chronic kidney disease (reduced EPO production)
Malignancies: Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, cervical cancer
Heart failure, chronic liver disease, and post‑surgical inflammation

sections.p: Patients usually report gradual fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, and pallor. Physical exam may show mild tachycardia, systolic flow murmur, and signs of the underlying chronic disease.
b: Pallor of conjunctivae and nail beds
Mild tachycardia without hypotension
Systolic ejection murmur due to high output state
Signs of underlying condition (e.g., lymphadenopathy in TB, joint swelling in RA)

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm anaemia, assess iron handling, and identify the inflammatory driver.

t.b: What is red cell morphology? – Shows normocytic, normochromic cells, helping exclude sideroblastic or thalassaemia.
Is iron storage adequate? – Ferritin ≥100 µg/L supports ACD; low ferritin suggests iron deficiency.

t.a: HIV rapid test or ELISA (if not known)
t.b: Is HIV a contributing chronic infection? – Positive test directs antiretroviral therapy.

t.a: Chest X‑ray or sputum GeneXpert (if TB suspected)
t.b: Is active TB present? – Radiographic infiltrates or positive GeneXpert confirm TB, prompting anti‑TB treatment.

t.a: Urine microscopy for schistosome eggs (if endemic)
t.b: Is schistosomiasis contributing? – Detection of eggs guides praziquantel therapy.
Is chronic kidney disease present? – Reduced eGFR indicates need for EPO‑stimulating agents later.

sections.p: Severe anaemia can precipitate cardiac failure, tissue hypoxia, and increased mortality, especially in patients with co‑existing heart or lung disease.
b: Hb <8 g/dL with chest pain or syncope
Rapid drop in Hb >2 g/dL over 48 h
New onset heart failure signs (pulmonary oedema, peripheral oedema)
Severe dyspnoea out of proportion to known disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying inflammatory condition first; then provide supportive measures to improve haemoglobin while avoiding unnecessary iron.
b: Treat infection or inflammation (e.g., anti‑TB regimen, ART for HIV, disease‑modifying antirheumatic drugs for RA)
Consider oral or IV iron only if iron deficiency co‑exists (ferritin <30 µg/L)
Erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents (ESA) for CKD‑related ACD when Hb <10 g/dL and iron stores adequate
Blood transfusion for symptomatic severe anaemia or Hb <7 g/dL in unstable patients
Avoid routine iron supplementation in isolated ACD – may worsen infection

sections.p: Monitor haemoglobin, inflammatory markers, and response to therapy every 4–6 weeks; prevent recurrence by controlling chronic disease.
b: Repeat CBC and ferritin after 4 weeks of therapy
Track CRP/ESR to gauge inflammation control
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus in chronic liver/kidney disease
Educate patients on adherence to anti‑TB, ART, or DMARD regimens

sections.p: Several other microcytic or normocytic anaemias share laboratory features.
b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia – low ferritin, high TIBC
Thalassaemia trait – microcytosis, normal/high ferritin, family history
Sideroblastic anaemia – high ferritin, ringed sideroblasts on marrow

sections.p: Inflammation can mask iron deficiency and alter typical iron studies.
b: Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant; may be high despite true iron deficiency
Transferrin saturation can be low in both ACD and iron deficiency – need ferritin to differentiate
CRP elevation may falsely elevate serum iron in acute infection; interpret with clinical context

whenToSeekHelp: Severe symptomatic anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL) with chest pain, syncope, or acute heart failure
Rapid haemoglobin fall >2 g/dL in 48 h
Unexplained haemodynamic instability despite treatment of underlying disease

faq.q: Why is ferritin high in anaemia of chronic disease?
faq.a: Inflammatory cytokines increase hepcidin, which traps iron in macrophages and raises ferritin as an acute‑phase protein.
Only if true iron deficiency co‑exists; otherwise iron can fuel pathogens and does not correct the anaemia.

faq.q: When should erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents be used?
faq.a: In CKD‑related ACD when Hb remains <10 g/dL despite optimal treatment of the underlying cause and iron stores are adequate.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with newly diagnosed HIV presents with Hb 9 g/dL, low serum iron and ferritin 150 µg/L. What is the next step? — Assess for concurrent iron deficiency (ferritin <30 µg/L) and start ART; avoid iron unless deficiency proven.
Why is transferrin saturation not increased in ACD despite low serum iron? — Hepcidin reduces transferrin release and iron export, keeping saturation low or normal.

A child with sickle cell disease has Hb 7 g/dL, ferritin 120 µg/L, and high reticulocyte count. How does this differ from ACD? — Reticulocytosis indicates marrow hyperactivity, typical of haemolysis, not the blunted response of ACD.
When is blood transfusion indicated in ACD? — When Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms of tissue hypoxia or cardiovascular compromise, or when rapid decline threatens organ perfusion.
Explain why oral iron can worsen infection in ACD. — Excess free iron fuels bacterial growth; inflammation already sequesters iron, so supplementation may increase pathogen proliferation.
A patient on anti‑TB therapy still has Hb 9 g/dL after 2 months. What additional measure may help? — Consider adding an ESA if renal function is impaired and iron stores are sufficient.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral for a patient with ACD? — Development of chest pain, syncope, or new heart failure signs indicating severe anaemia.
